Telescope resolution demo

How to use it: pick a telescope, or set the aperture and wavelength yourself, then change the separation of the two stars. The left panel is the true sky; the right panel is what the telescope makes of it. Use Set separation to place the stars at the Rayleigh limit, then watch them merge as you shrink the aperture. Switch to the test pattern to see fine detail wash out in the same way.

Seeing is the blurring from turbulence in Earth's atmosphere, typically 0.5–1 arcsec at good sites. Leave it at zero for a space telescope or an ideal adaptive-optics system. Wavelength presets for the telescopes can be changed afterwards.

Resolution readout

According to the Rayleigh criterion, two point sources are just resolved when their separation is about θ ≈ 1.22 λ / D. At that separation the dip between the two peaks is about 74% of the peak brightness.

Brightness along the line through the sources

Why bigger telescopes see finer detail. Light passing through a circular aperture spreads into an Airy pattern: a bright core ringed by faint rings. The core's angular radius, 1.22 λ / D, is the diffraction limit. Every point in the sky is smeared into this pattern, so detail finer than that blends together.

  • Bigger D, finer detail. Doubling the aperture halves the limit.
  • Shorter λ, finer detail. At 2 µm, JWST's 6.5 m mirror has a limit of about 0.077″, coarser than Hubble's 0.058″ at 550 nm, despite the bigger mirror.
  • The atmosphere. From the ground, turbulence usually limits visible-light images to 0.5–1″ whatever the size. Try the seeing slider with the VLT. Space telescopes and adaptive optics get closer to the diffraction limit.
  • Interferometry. A single 12 m ALMA dish resolves only about 27″ at 1.3 mm. ALMA combines many dishes, and its resolution then depends on the distance between them (up to about 16 km), not the size of one dish.
  • Simplified model. Equal-brightness stars, a clear circular aperture (no central obstruction), no noise, and an exact calculation of the image from the aperture's transfer function. When a telescope is sharper than the picture's pixels, the image is limited by the display.
